---
title: "Dependency injection"
verify: output # scripting assembly names are normalized by the verifier
---

Dependency injection (DI) is one of the ways to implement the dependency inversion principle.

Dependency injection in practice means that the external types the class depends on are passed in from an external source, instead of being created in the class itself.

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Implementing DI helps by making the code more configurable, because only the type that is being injected can be changed in a single place, instead of the concrete instantiation everywhere.

Another place where DI is helpful is in testing. DI makes the code more configurable so it is easier to pass fake class implementations to isolate the type under testing.
:::

***

Dependency inversion as one of the SOLID principles:

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    A[High-level Module] -->|depends on| B[Abstraction]
    C[Low-level Module] -->|depends on| B[Abstraction]
```

## Example 1

Let's say there is an interface `IStudentRepository` like this:

```csharp
interface IStudentRepository
{
    Task SaveStudentAsync(Student student);
    Task<List<Student>> GetStudentsAsync();
}
```

::: {.notes}
The `IStudentRepository` interface does not specify how or where the students are stored, the interface just deals with what it can do - store and retrieve the students. There are multiple legitimate ways how the interface can be implemented, so there are multiple possible classes to use in place of this interface.
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
For this example let's say there is a class `FileStudentRepository` which implements the interface `IStudentRepository` and saves as well as retrieves students from a file.

Without using DI, an option how to acquire an instance of `IStudentRepository` in the `StudentsController` class would be by simply manually instantiating `FileStudentRepository` inside the constructor.
:::

***

```csharp
public class StudentsController : ControllerBase
{
    private readonly IStudentRepository _repository;

    public StudentsController()
    {
        _repository = new FileStudentRepository();
    }

    public async Task SaveStudent(StudentDto dto)
    {
        await _repository.SaveStudentAsync(new Student(dto));
    }
}
```

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
It is a fair argument to say, that this works pretty well if this is the only place where `IStudentRepository` is used.

If we were certain that the alternative implementation of the interface would not be viable, then this would also work fine. The same goes if we were sure that the exact implementation wouldn't need to be switched during the runtime.
:::

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
However, the acquisition of an instance implementing `IStudentRepository` could be done differently. Specifically - using the dependency injection pattern. Using DI, the construction of an instance would happen some place else, and the instance would be simply provided via one of few options, based on what DI framework is used.
:::

***

`StudentsController` class with `IStudentRepository` injected via constructor:

```csharp
public class StudentsController : ControllerBase
{
    private readonly IStudentRepository _repository;

    public StudentsController(IStudentRepository repository)
    {
        _repository = repository;
    }

    public async Task SaveStudent(StudentDto dto)
    {
        await _repository.SaveStudentAsync(new Student(dto));
    }
}
```

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
With injection like this, the `StudentsController` becomes more modular. Exact implementation can be swapped during the class construction time. Also, since the `StudentsController` doesn't know which exact implementation of `IStudentRepository` is used, one could argue that the abstractions are better isolated.
:::

***

```csharp
// Since C# 12 the same can be written more concisely using a primary constructor.
// The constructor parameter is available in the whole class body.
public class StudentsController(IStudentRepository repository) : ControllerBase
{
    public async Task SaveStudent(StudentDto dto)
    {
        await repository.SaveStudentAsync(new Student(dto));
    }
}
```

## Example 2

This example follows the idea from the Example 1, but takes a look at the problem from a different angle.

Let's say we have a class which is responsible for calculating students grades:

```csharp
class GradesCalculator
{
    private readonly string _connectionStringFacultyA = "<something>";
    private readonly string _connectionStringFacultyB = "<something>";

    public double CalculateFinalGrade(string studentId)
    {
        List<int> grades;

        if (studentId.EndsWith("A"))
        {
            var dbContext = new FacultyADbContext(_connectionStringFacultyA);
            grades = dbContext.Students
                .Where(x => x.Id == studentId)
                .SelectMany(x => x.Grades)
                .ToList();
        }
        else if (studentId.EndsWith("B"))
        {
            var dbContext = new FacultyBDbContext(_connectionStringFacultyB);
            grades = dbContext.Grades
                .Where(x => x.StudentId == studentId)
                .Select(x => x.Value)
                .ToList();
        }
        else
        {
            throw new ArgumentException($"Unknown faculty of student {studentId}");
        }

        return grades.Average();
    }
}
```

::: {.notes}
What is happening in the example class above:

- Retrieval logic differs slightly based on which faculty the student is studying at.
- Different classes are needed to access data based on faculty.
- Different parameters are needed to create classes for data access.
- Hypothetically if the `GradesCalculator` had more methods, which were working with students data, then the same `if/else` blocks could proliferate.
:::

***

What improvements could be done using DI in such case:

1. Standardize the classes for data accessing using an interface:

```csharp
interface IStudentDataRepository
{
    List<int> GetGrades(string studentId);
}

class FacultyADbContext : IStudentDataRepository
{
    // <..> some boilerplate and implementation details

    public List<int> GetGrades(string studentId)
    {
        return Students
            .Where(x => x.Id == studentId)
            .SelectMany(x => x.Grades)
            .ToList();
    }
}

// Same for FacultyBDbContext
```

***

2. Inject data access logic into the `GradesCalculator`:

```csharp
class GradesCalculator
{
    private readonly IStudentDataRepository _repository;

    public GradesCalculator(IStudentDataRepository repository)
    {
        _repository = repository;
    }

    public double CalculateFinalGrade(string studentId)
    {
        List<int> grades = _repository.GetGrades(studentId);

        return grades.Average();
    }
}
```

::: {.notes}
Replacing the `if/else` on faculty with an interface, whose implementation is chosen somewhere else, is called the "Strategy pattern". Each faculty's data access is a separate strategy, and `GradesCalculator` works with whichever one it is given.
:::

***

3. Wire everything up in the DI framework config:

```csharp
// Program.cs
// <...>
// Keyed services (.NET 8+) register several implementations of the same interface
builder.Services.AddKeyedScoped<IStudentDataRepository, FacultyADbContext>("A");
builder.Services.AddKeyedScoped<IStudentDataRepository, FacultyBDbContext>("B");

// The key is only known at request time, so a factory picks the implementation
builder.Services.AddScoped<Func<string, IStudentDataRepository>>(sp =>
    faculty => sp.GetRequiredKeyedService<IStudentDataRepository>(faculty));
// <...>
app.MapGet(
    "/grades/{studentId}",
    (string studentId, Func<string, IStudentDataRepository> repositoryFor) =>
    {
        var faculty = studentId[^1..]; // last character of the id
        var calculator = new GradesCalculator(repositoryFor(faculty));
        return calculator.CalculateFinalGrade(studentId);
    }
);
// <...>
```

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
When the key is known at compile time, a keyed service can be injected directly using the `[FromKeyedServices("A")]` attribute on the parameter. Here the key depends on the request, so a factory is needed. Before .NET 8 the same was done with a `Func` factory that resolved the concrete classes with a `switch`.

### Was it worth it?

When looking at `GradesCalculator` class in isolation, it did indeed become less complicated. On the other hand the `Program.cs` now has configuration logic that wasn't needed before. Depending on specific use case for which DI is being implemented for, varying amount and complexities of code can be removed or would have to be added.

It is one of the responsibilities of a Software Engineer to figure out the right balance and decide if introducing some design pattern like DI into the solution is a net-positive or not.
:::

## Benefits of DI

- Forces the code to be more testable (easier to pass some `Fake` implementation for the classes under testing).
- Single instance can be reused by different classes in the same request scope.
- Code can be more configurable and modular.

## Problems with DI

Main problem is not with the DI pattern itself, but that it has a tendency to provoke overengineering and indirection.

While it is nice that you are not *forced to care* how exactly the dependency is implemented, sometimes you *need* to know how that dependency works. DI provokes extra hoops to jump through until you find the actual source.

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
## Further considerations

Dependencies can be resolved recursively, which means that the `FileStudentRepository` class can be injecting dependencies it needs as well. The only nuance is that while the dependencies can be injected recursively, the top most class must be instantiated some other way. This is where the dependency injection frameworks come into play.

DI frameworks allow to configure the concrete implementations for injected types, their lifetimes and more. .NET has the `Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection` framework, which is baked into ASP.NET and generic host applications, however there are alternative frameworks like `Autofac` and more.

Next sections explore how to create a simple dependency injection library yourself and how to use the standard Microsoft DI framework in ASP.NET.
:::

## Building a DI framework

To create a simplest homemade DI framework there are 2 obvious problems that need to be solved:

1. How to know what dependencies the class has?
2. How to instantiate the top-most class in the tree?

For the 1st problem a language feature "reflection" is typically used. Reflection allows to get the meta information about the types and assemblies during the runtime. It can also be used to instantiate the type dynamically, just by knowing its assembly and name.

For the 2nd problem a service locator pattern will be used. Service locator simply takes in a type as an argument and returns the instance that satisfies the type requirement for the given argument.

### Reflection

Types that are used for reflection are located in `System.Reflection` namespace.

Reflection can be used to access the member information on the type, get the types in assembly, get the attributes and their values and more. Here we will focus on the essentials.

```{.csharp}
// Let's define a type that will be used to inspect using the reflection

public class Person
{
    public string Name { get; init; }
    public int Age { get; init; }

    public Person(string name, int age)
    {
        Name = name;
        Age = age;
    }

    public void SayHi()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Hi, my name is {Name} and I'm {Age} years old.");
    }
}
```

***

To start reflecting on the `Person` class a type of this class will have to be acquired first:

```{.csharp}
using System.Reflection;

// Type can be assigned during a compile time:
var typeCompileTime = typeof(Person);

// Or it can be assigned during a runtime:
var typeRuntime = new Person("John", 30).GetType();

// In any case, they are the same type
Console.WriteLine(typeCompileTime == typeRuntime);
```

***

```{.csharp}
// Just for brevity
var type = typeCompileTime;

// Get all the properties of the type
var properties = type.GetProperties();

Console.WriteLine($"Properties of the type {type.Name}:");
foreach (var property in properties)
{
    Console.WriteLine(property.Name);
}
```

***

```{.csharp}
// In this example Person class has no public fields:
var fields = type.GetFields();
foreach (var field in fields)
{
    Console.WriteLine(field.Name);
}
```

***

```{.csharp}
// But we know that it has properties, which should have private backing fields generated by the compiler.
// To access them, some additional flags indicating that we want to access private members are required:
var fieldsWithPrivate = type.GetFields(BindingFlags.NonPublic | BindingFlags.Instance);
foreach (var field in fieldsWithPrivate)
{
    Console.WriteLine(field.Name);
}
```

***

Although we only defined the `SayHi` method, the class has more of them. Some of them come inherited implicitly from the `object` base class, others (like `get_*` and `set_*`) are created during the compilation time.

```{.csharp}
// Get all the methods of the type
var methods = type.GetMethods();
foreach (var method in methods)
{
    Console.WriteLine(method.Name);
}
```

***

```{.csharp}
// Reflection can be used to call the methods as well:
var instance = new Person("John", 30);
var methodInfo = type.GetMethod("SayHi");

// Second parameter is an array of arguments, which the SayHi method does not have
methodInfo.Invoke(instance, null);
```

***

```{.csharp}
// Similarly reflection can be used to get and set the property values

// Get the property info
var propertyInfo = type.GetProperty("Name");

// Get the value of the property
var value = propertyInfo.GetValue(instance);

Console.WriteLine(value);

// Set the value of the property.
// Name is init-only, so `instance.Name = "Jane"` would not compile,
// but reflection bypasses such compile time restrictions (as well as private access).
propertyInfo.SetValue(instance, "Jane");

Console.WriteLine(instance.Name);
```

***

```{.csharp}
// Reflection can be used to obtain information about the types in assembly:
var assembly = Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly();

var types = assembly.GetTypes();

Console.WriteLine($"Types in the assembly {assembly.FullName}:");
foreach (var t in types)
{
    Console.WriteLine(t.Name);
}

// We know there is a Person type, but it is not listed: the script runner compiles
// every cell into a separate assembly, and Person lives in the first cell's assembly.
```

***

```{.csharp}
// If the type is defined in the same cell, it is in the same assembly and gets listed.

public class Person
{
    public string Name { get; init; }
    public int Age { get; init; }

    public Person(string name, int age)
    {
        Name = name;
        Age = age;
    }

    public void SayHi()
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"Hi, my name is {Name} and I'm {Age} years old.");
    }
}

var assembly = Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly();

var types = assembly.GetTypes();

Console.WriteLine($"Types in the assembly {assembly.FullName}:");
foreach (var t in types)
{
    Console.WriteLine(t.Name);
}
```

***

```{.csharp}
// Reflection can also be used to get the information about the constructors of the type
var constructors = typeof(Person).GetConstructors();

Console.WriteLine($"Constructors of the type {typeof(Person).Name}:");
foreach (var constructor in constructors)
{
    Console.WriteLine(constructor);
}
```

***

```{.csharp}
// Reflection can be used to instantiate the type completely dynamically
var personType = typeof(Person);

var constructor = personType.GetConstructors()[0];
var person = constructor.Invoke(new object[] { "John", 30 });

personType.GetMethod("SayHi").Invoke(person, null);
```

### DI framework implementation with Service Locator

Service locator is a design pattern to which you pass the type and get the instance back.

The simple interface for the pattern can look like this:

```csharp
public class ServiceLocator
{
    public T GetInstance<T>() { }
}
```

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
For this example assume that there is an interface `IStudentRepository` and `FileStudentRepository` which implements the interface. Our DI library will be simple and convention based: it will search the given assembly for a type that is assignable to the type requested by the constructor.

Service locator is fine inside a DI framework, which is what is being built here. However, when application classes call the service locator themselves to get their dependencies, it is considered an anti-pattern: the dependencies are hidden inside the method bodies instead of being visible in the constructor.
:::

***

```{.csharp}
public class Student { }

public interface IStudentRepository
{
    void Save(Student student);
}

public class StudentController
{
    private readonly IStudentRepository _studentRepository;

    public StudentController(IStudentRepository studentRepository)
    {
        _studentRepository = studentRepository;
    }

    public void SaveStudent(Student student)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Saving student in the controller");
        _studentRepository.Save(student);
    }
}

public class FileStudentRepository : IStudentRepository
{
    public void Save(Student student)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Saving student to a file");
    }
}
```

***

```{.csharp}
class ServiceLocator
{
    private readonly Assembly _assembly;

    // The assembly in which the implementations are searched for
    public ServiceLocator(Assembly assembly)
    {
        _assembly = assembly;
    }

    // Because the reflection happens at runtime, there is no way of being type safe then.
    // This adds a generic layer and casting to convert the object to the desired type.
    public T GetInstance<T>() where T : class
    {
        return (T)GetInstance(typeof(T));
    }

    private object GetInstance(Type requestedType)
    {
        // Find the first non-abstract class that is assignable to the requested type
        var type = _assembly.GetTypes()
            .FirstOrDefault(x => x.IsClass && !x.IsAbstract && x.IsAssignableTo(requestedType));
        if (type == null)
        {
            throw new InvalidOperationException($"Cannot locate implementation for type {requestedType}");
        }

        // Just use the first constructor, might not work well if there were more than one
        var ctor = type.GetConstructors()[0];

        // Constructor can require other types to be injected, so they are resolved recursively.
        // Note: a circular dependency (A needs B, B needs A) would end in a stack overflow.
        var ctorParams = ctor.GetParameters()
            .Select(param => GetInstance(param.ParameterType))
            .ToArray();

        return ctor.Invoke(ctorParams);
    }
}
```

***

```{.csharp}
// Test it out
var serviceLocator = new ServiceLocator(typeof(StudentController).Assembly);
var studentController = serviceLocator.GetInstance<StudentController>();
studentController.SaveStudent(new Student());
```

### Testing with a fake

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Because `StudentController` receives its dependency instead of creating it, a test can pass in a fake implementation and check how the controller used it, without touching any files.
:::

```{.csharp}
public class FakeStudentRepository : IStudentRepository
{
    public List<Student> Saved { get; } = new();

    public void Save(Student student)
    {
        Saved.Add(student);
    }
}

var fakeRepository = new FakeStudentRepository();
var controller = new StudentController(fakeRepository);

controller.SaveStudent(new Student());

Console.WriteLine($"Students saved: {fakeRepository.Saved.Count}");
```

## Usage of Microsoft DI in .NET

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
The actual purpose built DI libraries are much more capable than the one in the example above. ASP.NET comes with Microsoft DI library out of the box and it is a solid choice to use for most scenarios.

Since the controller or an endpoint definition are natural entry points for most cases in the ASP.NET application, there is no need to use things like service locators. To start using DI it is enough to create a constructor with the required type (or add an argument when using endpoints).

For DI framework to know which type will have to be injected, it will have to be manually registered.

ASP.NET application will have templated code looking something like this:
:::

```csharp
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

// The builder is of WebApplicationBuilder or similar type.
// It has property `.Services` with methods needed to register services to the container.

builder.Services.AddSingleton<IStudentRepository, FileStudentRepository>();
```

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
In the example above there is everything that needs to be done to start injecting the `IStudentRepository` inside the controller.
:::

***

One important thing to know are the lifetimes of instances. They can be:

- Singleton (`AddSingleton()`).
- Scoped (`AddScoped()`).
- Transient (`AddTransient()`).

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
Singletons use a single instance for all the injections within the application lifetime. For example, `ILogger<T>` is registered as a singleton.

Scoped uses a single instance for the single scope. In ASP.NET the single scope is 1 HTTP request. However if this DI framework were to be used for a console app, then the scopes could be manually configured to mean whatever makes sense in that case. From a practical point of view in ASP.NET this means that if several classes use the same `DbContext` (registered as scoped by `AddDbContext()`), then the exact same instance of `DbContext` is injected into them during a single request, and they share its change tracking.

Transient injects a new instance for every single injection. This means that if there are a couple of classes injected into a constructor and they both require the same transient service, then different instances are injected into them.
:::

***

```csharp
// Captive dependency: a longer-lived service holds on to a shorter-lived one.

builder.Services.AddScoped<IStudentRepository, DbStudentRepository>();
builder.Services.AddSingleton<StudentCache>();

class StudentCache(IStudentRepository repository) // singleton
{
    // The scoped repository (and its DbContext) is created once and then kept
    // for the whole application lifetime, shared between all requests.
}
```

::: {.content-visible unless-format="revealjs"}
A service should only depend on services with the same or longer lifetime. Injecting a scoped service into a singleton turns it into a singleton in practice, which for a `DbContext` means it is shared between concurrent requests even though it is not thread safe. ASP.NET validates scopes in the Development environment and throws an exception on startup when it detects such a dependency.
:::
